extracted.intended_audience: educated readers (theologians, natural philosophers, or lay apologetes) aiming to construct or evaluate anatomy-based arguments for divine design
extracted.subtask_description: How to build and evaluate a natural-theology (design) argument using anatomical observations, experiments, and physiological reasoning; oriented to persuading skeptics by correlating empirical facts with teleological interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlate scripture with anatomical fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that biblical expressions about generation (e.g., 'Children proceed from the Loins') correspond accurately to anatomical structures and functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use anatomical knowledge (e.g. location of seminal vessels, circulation through arteries O and P) to argue that the Scriptural text 'speaks with compleat Knowledge of the Cause' and could not come from an uninspired person; point to specific texts (Gen. chap. xxx; 1 Kings chap. viii; 2 Chron. vi.9) and anatomical features as parallel evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to authoritative anatomists and figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on and cite the enquiries and observations of noted anatomists (Willis, Vieussens, Verheyen, Malpighi, Bellini, Bergerus, Bartholinus, Pacchioni) and their figures to establish anatomical facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage the reader to 'consult the large Figures of Mr. Vieussens' or 'Bergerus' and to base conviction upon the experiments and dissections reported by these authorities; reference specific plates (Tab. IV. Fig. 3, 6, 8) and empirical corpuses (e.g. dissections of 400 bodies over fifteen years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate complexity and particularity of nerve branching
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that the innumerable fine branches of the nerves each perform particular functions and that not one, 'yea, not the smallest Branch or Sprig of them but has its Use'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use detailed anatomical illustrations (Tab. IV Fig. 6) and the sheer multiplicity and precise disposition of nerve branches to argue that such arrangement could not be due to chance; ask whether an unexperienced eye's perception of irregularity is compatible with purposive disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct experiments to establish physiological mechanisms (nervous juice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adduce and, where possible, reproduce experiments (Bellini, Malpighi, Bergerus) that demonstrate a viscous 'nervous juice' (succus nervosus) running through nerves rather than the passage of a volatile 'animal spirit'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe experiments: press the nerve of the midriff in a recently dead creature to displace fluid and observe restoration/resumption of motion; press the end of a great nerve (e.g. in an ox) to see it swell and exude a viscous, turpentine-like liquor. Use repeated, corroborated experimental results as firm proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refute alternative explanations by empirical and chemical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Challenge rival hypotheses (e.g. that 'animal spirits' or a wind/spirit produce motion) by pointing to the implausibility regarding speed and the physical nature of nerves and by citing chemical examples where non-volatile mixtures produce violent motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring up chemical experiments (mixing oil of vitriol and salt of tartar; gunpowder; glass of antimony) to show that swift and violent motions do not require a volatile spirit; argue that the moist substance of brain and nerves is ill-suited to convey a wind-like principle at lightning speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain coordinated, teleological design among organs
rubrics_metrics.description: Show how nerve distributions perform coordinated functions (e.g. nerves of hearing send branches to ear muscles, eyes, speech organs; nerves of tasting send branches to mastication muscles, glands, nose and eyes) to support the claim of wise design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete functional chains (hearing → erecting ear → looking; taste → mastication → saliva glands → moistening mouth) to demonstrate purposive coordination; emphasize readiness and immediacy of these coordinated responses as evidence of contrivance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish involuntary vs voluntary nervous control as evidence of design
rubrics_metrics.description: Point out that some nerves (originating from the spinal marrow forepart) are governed by will (voluntary muscles) while others (from the hind-part/medulla) act incessantly without will (involuntary), and argue that this separation is purposeful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples: limbs governed by will; heart, respiration, stomach, intestines governed involuntarily; show how this division suits life’s needs (e.g. respiration must continue during sleep), supporting the contention of wise, intentional arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fail-safes and redundant innervation as evidence of providential design
rubrics_metrics.description: Highlight instances where multiple nerves contribute to the same organ (e.g., Vagus and intercostal nerves supplying the heart and stomach) so that if one supply fails the other sustains function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point to plexuses formed by concurrence of different nerves (e.g. plexus E composed of vagus and intercostal branches) and interpret such redundancy as deliberate provision to preserve vital functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate necessity and indispensability of structures via experimental lesioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use experimental evidence (e.g., tying an artery or cutting a nerve results in loss of motion) to show the essential roles of arteries, veins, and nerves for motion and life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Bartholinus's experiments: binding an artery or a nerve renders a limb void of motion; use such cause-effect demonstrations to argue that organs are formed for particular ends (support, motion, procreation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe and interpret lymphatic and glandular specializations
rubrics_metrics.description: Detail the vas a lymphatica, their valves, communications with glands, discharge into chyle receptacle, and glands’ roles in separating juices with distinct tastes and functions (saline urine, tears, sweat, bile, milk, saliva).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observations from dissections and injections (e.g., quicksilver into lymphatics) and reference Tab. IV Fig. 8; argue that the specific separation of humours and their consequent properties indicate design rather than chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogue membranes' multiple functions and use them as design evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: List the membranes’ roles: covering parts (pleura, peritoneum), forming tubes and vessels, fastening parts together (mesentery), dividing cavities (mediastinum), acting as instruments of feeling, and containing muscular fibres that effect peristaltic-like motions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the multiplicity of membrane functions as cumulative evidence: their structural variety and functional importance (including muscular contraction to propel contents) make purposeless origin implausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propose plausible mechanisms for poorly understood phenomena (e.g., dura mater contraction)
rubrics_metrics.description: When direct mechanism is unknown, advance plausible physiological hypotheses (such as contraction of the dura mater driving nervous juice into nerves) and show how they coherently explain observed facts (e.g., why tied nerves do not swell).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present hypotheses modestly ('I leave this Matter to farther Enquiry') but show how they resolve otherwise unintelligible practical cases; use the hypothesis to predict phenomena (e.g., tying a nerve would stop peristaltic-like protrusion) and invite experimental verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize structural flexibility and adaptation to movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Point out that arteries, veins, nerves, and lymphatic tubes are constructed with flexibility appropriate to joints and extension (so they operate both when limbs are bent and stretched).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observable adaptation (tubes composed of membranes that accommodate bending at elbow/fingers) as another line of teleological inference: the fit between form and mechanical requirement argues for design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the muscular and skeletal arrangement as final corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: Argue that the insertion of muscles into bones, the exact adaptation of bones for limbs and joints, and the fine fibres that produce amazing strength form an additional, compelling set of facts supporting wise contrivance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve fuller detail for further anatomical enquiry (as the author does when transitioning to muscles) but treat the musculo-skeletal system as the culminating empirical support for design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine empirical demonstration with moral/rhetorical appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: After assembling anatomical and experimental evidence, conclude with a moral exhortation: that such facts should move the enquirer from doubt to gratitude and worship of the Creator, and that denial in the face of these facts is morally and intellectually culpable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use rhetorical questions, contrasts between the 'unhappy Atheist' and the 'more happy' believer, and appeals to conscience and self-reflection to convert empirical conviction into moral/religious commitment.
